ingredients.item: live abalone in the shell , or 8 cleaned abalone meats with shells reserved
toasted sesame seeds , finely sliced scallion
Steamed rice , a light lettuce salad, and the table's best drinks — this is a celebration record

instructions.heading: Step 1
instructions.action: A spoon of butter into each shell's hollow, the scored abalone over it, shells to the moderate fire in their cradle. Four minutes, no touching.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the butter bubbles around the meat's edge, the scores open pale, and the surface turns from glassy to matte. The smell is butter and sweet ocean.

instructions.heading: Step 2
instructions.action: Baste each meat with the garlicky butter from its own shell, one more minute, off the fire while the foot still has spring at a fingertip press.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the pull test is the record: pressed, the meat springs back slowly (tender-window) — a fast hard snap-back means it tightened past the window; if it never firmed at all, thirty seconds more. The test piece cut thick: resistant-tender, buttery, ocean-sweet — abalone's texture is the dish, and "just right" is a real, findable 60 seconds.

instructions.heading: Step 3
instructions.action: Sesame and scallion over each, the shells straight to the table in the cradle, drinks already poured.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: eating test: the whole meat in two or three thick bites off a small fork or the tip of a chopstick's handle, rice after — and the shell's butter-juice pooled beneath is the cook's sip, the oldest gratuity at the coast.

storageNotes: Live abalone keeps 1–2 days in the fridge in a damp cloth over ice — never submerged in fresh water. Cooked, 1 day; this is an eat-in-the-minute record.

Variations: a drop of gochujang butter (#SF12's sauce) in each shell for the spicy fork; the same butter on the oyster record's cups; the cleaned trim and liver into the next morning's jeonbok porridge — the full-use tradition.
